note_claims.claim: The patient is reviewing diabetes care following a hypoglycaemic episode.
The patient experienced a hypoglycaemic episode about three months ago after skipping lunch while gardening.
The patient's daughter (who has type 1 diabetes) found him confused during the episode.
The patient's daughter measured the capillary glucose at 2.8 mmol/L during the episode.
The patient recovered from the episode within 15 minutes.
The patient experiences occasional pre-meal wobbliness.
The patient drives locally.
The patient has no neuropathic symptoms.
The patient has no visual problems.
The patient is prescribed Metformin 1g twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Gliclazide 80 mg twice daily.
The patient is prescribed Atorvastatin 20 mg.
The patient is prescribed Ramipril 5 mg.
The patient's pedal pulses are palpable.
The patient's ankle brachial pressure index is 1.0 bilaterally.
Monofilament sensation is normal in both feet.
The patient has a callus under the right first metatarsal head.
The patient's blood pressure is 138/84.
The patient's weight is 91 kg.
The patient's HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol, which is up from 58.
The patient's eGFR is 52, which is stable.
The patient has Type 2 diabetes with recent hypoglycaemia on gliclazide.
The patient has stable CKD stage 3a.
The plan is to continue gliclazide 80 mg twice daily.
The plan is to start empagliflozin 10 mg once daily.
The plan is to refer the patient to a podiatrist for the callus.
The plan is to book a retinal screening.
The plan is to review the patient in three months with repeat HbA1c and kidney tests.
Safety netting includes checking blood glucose before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
Safety netting includes not driving if blood sugar is below 5 mmol/L.
Safety netting includes keeping fast-acting glucose in the car.
Safety netting includes stopping empagliflozin if the patient is vomiting, has diarrhoea, or is unable to eat and drink.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician greeted Mr Elsworth-Mahmood.
Patient's daughter, Yasmin, requested the visit due to an incident last week.
Relative greeted the clinician.
Patient experienced symptoms including being sweaty, shaky, and unable to think straight.
The hypoglycaemic episode occurred on Tuesday because it was bin day and the patient had skipped lunch.
The patient had been in the garden all morning and skipped lunch.
Relative found the patient confused and identified it as a hypo due to her own type 1 diabetes.
Relative gave the patient orange juice and biscuits.
The patient recovered within about fifteen minutes.
Relative used her meter and measured the capillary glucose at 2.8.
Patient reports feeling a bit wobbly before tea sometimes.
Patient drives to the shops and to his allotment.
Patient confirmed he was not driving that day.
Clinician checked medications and found the patient is on metformin 1 gram twice a day.
Patient confirmed the Metformin dose.
Clinician checked medications and found the patient is on gliclazide 80 milligrams twice a day.
Patient confirmed the Gliclazide dosing schedule (morning and teatime).
Clinician checked medications and found the patient is on Atorvastatin 20 milligrams and ramipril 5 milligrams.
Patient confirmed all listed medications.
Clinician asked about allergies.
Patient reported no known drug allergies.
Clinician asked about problems with feet, tingling, or numbness.
Patient reported his feet have been fine.
Relative reported having pins and needles and getting it in her hands at night, suspecting carpal tunnel.
Clinician addressed Yasmin but decided to stick with the patient (dad) regarding foot problems.
Patient reported no problems with his eyesight and had received his eye screening letter.
Patient's HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol, up from 58 last time.
Patient's kidney function (eGFR) is 52, which is about the same as before.
Patient asked if the results were bad.
Clinician noted that sugar control has drifted up a little, but the hypo worries him more.
Clinician checked the patient's feet and noted that pulses are fine in both feet.
Clinician noted there is a bit of hard skin and a callus under the ball of the patient's left foot, by the big toe.
Clinician noted the patient's blood pressure is 138 over 84.
Clinician noted the patient's weight is 91 kilos.
Clinician suggested reducing gliclazide to 80 milligrams in the morning only and stopping the teatime dose.
Clinician suggested adding empagliflozin 10 milligrams once a day.
Clinician advised stopping empagliflozin when unwell and not eating or drinking (e.g., with vomiting or diarrhoea).
Clinician advised checking blood sugar before driving and every two hours on long journeys.
Clinician advised not to drive if blood sugar is below five.
Clinician advised keeping some sugary snacks in the car.
Relative offered to get glucose tablets for the patient.
Clinician offered to refer the patient to the podiatrist for the callus.
Clinician advised the patient to book his eye screening.
Clinician scheduled a follow-up appointment in three months with a repeat HbA1c and kidney test.
